data.title: Považská Bystrica – Dedovec, a fortified Slavic settlement
data.excerpt: The fortified Slavic settlement on Dedovec in Považská Bystrica, excavated in 1957–1958, remains the best-explored site of its period in the central Váh region. It existed from the end of the 8th to the first half of the 10th century; 54 features were investigated over an area of 57 × 46 m, and instead of the usual timber-and-earth rampart its inhabitants surrounded it with a timber palisade.

blocks.alt: The find site on Dedovec in Považská Bystrica

children.text: The fortified settlement on Dedovec in Považská Bystrica was systematically excavated in 1957–1958 under the direction of A. Petrovský-Šichman. The settlement remains the best-explored one of this period in the central Váh region. The existence of this fortified Slavic settlement is defined as running from the end of the 8th to the first half of the 10th century. An earlier beginning of the occupation, or conversely its longer survival, cannot be demonstrated. The site, however, was not excavated in its entirety, so such a possibility cannot be entirely ruled out. The fact remains, though, that the original assumption of the director of the excavation, who placed the bulk of the occupation here considerably deeper in the past, was not confirmed.

In the course of the fieldwork, 54 features were investigated over an area measuring 57 × 46 m. For the most part these were various features sunk 10–45 cm into the ground, among which several types could be distinguished. Among the dwellings can be counted ground plans with an area of 4 m² and more, in which heating installations were found, usually placed in a corner. Either these were simple hearths without any treatment at all, or they were found to be lined or paved with stones; in one case the presence of a clay oven may perhaps be assumed. The interpretation of the smaller sunken features (under 4 m²) with a hearth is no longer so clear, but they were probably parts of larger dwelling structures. Heating installations were, moreover, also found outside the features and probably served several households, or even the whole settlement, as seasonal (summer) hearths, bread ovens and the like. Various possibilities of functional interpretation are offered by sunken features in which hearths are absent. In the case of ground plans with an area of over 4 m² these were mostly farm buildings. The precise determination of their purpose is, however, questionable, since the features did not contain finds that would make it possible. More difficult to interpret are the oval to ellipsoid pits with an area of 0.8–2.8 m². In two cases large parts of sizeable vessels were found in their fill. The find situation allows us to assume that the features served for storing food, the vessels evidently playing the role of storage vessels proper, protecting their contents against damp. A further pit with the remains of a somewhat smaller vessel and a more marked quantity of charcoal may have been the place where food was prepared or kept warm. A less well represented form of structural remains were deliberately created continuous surfaces of stones, which were concentrated above all on the southern side of the settlement. They can evidently be interpreted as parts of ground-level buildings, in which they served as paving, since we encounter this form of interior treatment as early as in earlier periods.

At the settlement at Dedovec the archaeologists did not succeed in discovering the remains of the typical timber-and-earth fortification that we are used to at other hillforts of the period of Great Moravia. Nevertheless, as for example Drahoslav Hulínek states in the book Bitka pri Bratislave v roku 907, this was not an “open” settlement: the inhabitants of Dedovec (the ancestors of today’s people of Považská Bystrica) surrounded the settlement with a timber palisade, which was evidently capable of ensuring their protection against less numerous or more weakly armed military groups.

Most of the movable finds from the Slavic fortified settlement on Dedovec are fragments of pottery vessels, coming almost exclusively from pot-shaped vessels of a wider range of forms. In their decoration it is above all horizontal grooves and wavy lines that are used; on the younger examples decoration created by multiple comb impressions also appears. Only sporadically (in two cases) did relief decoration in the form of encircling cordons appear as well. The second, incomparably less well represented type of ware were baking pans and bowls.

Metal, stone and bone objects make up, for understandable reasons, a considerably smaller percentage of the body of finds than pottery. In terms of function, however, they are more varied and reflect the different kinds of activity of the local population. The most numerous kind of iron objects are knives; of the twelve pieces recovered, 7 were preserved whole. The knives that were found were objects of everyday use with a universal application; in the cemeteries of the period they occur in both male and female graves, and only the larger examples can be regarded as weapons. A specific use is shown only by a small knife with a short blade passing into a long handle, which served as a

, which is matched by its exceptionally well-ground edge. The care of the body is also connected with toilet articles, represented by tweezers and by fragments of one or more double-sided bone combs. Besides the knives, objects of everyday use and tools for domestic craft activity are represented by iron needles, bone and iron awls, the fittings of wooden buckets, clay spindle whorls, stone whetstones and perhaps also a fragment of an iron fire-steel. This category evidently also includes a bone object which may have served for smoothing hides or the surface of pottery. Pottery production, however, was already the subject of a separate craft as well, which the technical and artistic level of part of the clay ware definitely proves. Among the specialised craft tools we may count small iron chisels, attested at the Dedovec settlement by at least one piece.

The basic form of subsistence of early medieval society was, however, agriculture. The keeping of domesticated animals is documented by the occurrence of bones and of objects made from them; the growing of cultivated plants is attested by the metal part of an ard that was found, by a fragment of an iron sickle and evidently also by an iron ring which, by analogy, probably served to fasten a scythe to its shaft. It is generally judged that in this period sickles were used for reaping cereals, while scythes served for mowing grass. A supplementary form of securing food was hunting and fishing. Arrowheads and a hook with a barb are connected with these activities. In the case of the arrowheads, however, these are objects that were not lacking in the armament of the warriors of the time either, and therefore the presence of a certain number of soldiers within the fortified settlement cannot be ruled out.

Relatively sparsely represented are the finds which otherwise make up the majority of the metal objects from settlements belonging to the developed phases of the Middle Ages, that is, structural fittings in the form of nails. A simple iron key, used for locking doors, occurred in isolation. Among the rare artefacts are also objects functioning as parts of dress and as jewellery. Three iron belt loops probably served to fasten the strap of a belt; to the adornment of women should be ascribed a bead of blue glass and, in view of the material used and the shape, evidently also a simple bronze ring with a pendant in the form of a chain link, which was probably an earring. It is of interest that among the finds from the period of Great Moravia there was also a dress brooch of the Late Roman period. It is quite possible that this was a kind of precious “antique” which adorned the dress of one of the women of Dedovec.

Besides Dedovec, artefacts have been found in several places in Považská Bystrica and its surroundings which suggest that other, evidently less important settlements also lay in the vicinity of Dedovec. In terms of its position in the landscape, the settlement on the terraces of the north-western slope of the castle hill at Považské Podhradie, for example, has a different character. The close proximity of the castle positively invites the thought that it was occupied, within the Middle Ages, already in this period, especially if the population there could have used its old rampart fortification of the La Tène period for their protection. So far, however, no finds have been established that could confirm such a supposition.
